claim: The striatum has an important role in spatial working memory.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest that the striatum has an important role in spatial working memory.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of existing literature, supported by citations throughout the introduction.

claim: Neural dynamics in the striatum have been described in tasks with short delay periods (1–4 s).
source: The neural dynamics in the striatum have been described in tasks with short delay periods (1–4 s), but remain largely uncharacterized for tasks with longer delay periods.
evidence: This statement references existing literature on striatal dynamics, as supported by citations in the introduction (Antzoulatos and Miller, 2011; Chiba et al., 2015; Hikosaka et al., 1989; Histed et al., 2009; Kawagoe et al., 1998; Kermadi and Joseph, 1995; Pasupathy and Miller, 2005).

claim: Striatal dynamics remain largely uncharacterized for tasks with longer delay periods.
source: The neural dynamics in the striatum have been described in tasks with short delay periods (1–4 s), but remain largely uncharacterized for tasks with longer delay periods.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract and introduction.

claim: Neurons in the dorsomedial striatum were activated sequentially during spatial working memory tasks.
source: We found that neurons were activated sequentially, with the sequences spanning the entire delay period.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and associated analyses.

claim: Sequential activity in the dorsomedial striatum spanned the entire delay period.
source: We found that neurons were activated sequentially, with the sequences spanning the entire delay period.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the heat-maps in Figure 4B showing sequential activation across 10s delay periods.

claim: Sequential activity was dissociated from stimulus encoding activity in the dorsomedial striatum.
source: Surprisingly, this sequential activity was dissociated from stimulus encoding activity, which was present in the same neurons, but preferentially appeared towards the onset of the delay period.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 5B-C showing lack of correlation between peak firing time and peak sample information time.

claim: Stimulus encoding activity was present in the same neurons that showed sequential activity.
source: Surprisingly, this sequential activity was dissociated from stimulus encoding activity, which was present in the same neurons, but preferentially appeared towards the onset of the delay period.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Figure 5B showing both firing rate sequences and sample information in the same neurons.

claim: Stimulus encoding activity preferentially appeared towards the onset of the delay period.
source: Surprisingly, this sequential activity was dissociated from stimulus encoding activity, which was present in the same neurons, but preferentially appeared towards the onset of the delay period.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5B and Figure 6A showing highest sample information and decoding accuracy at delay onset.

claim: Working memory is the ability to remember information over short periods of time and use the memory to guide ongoing behavior.
source: One of the most fundamental components of cognition is working memory, the ability to remember information over short periods of time and use the memory to guide ongoing behavior (Baddeley, 1992, 2003; Cowan, 2008).
evidence: This is a definition from established literature as indicated by the citations.

claim: Neural activity in prefrontal and parietal cortex encodes stimuli during the delay period of working memory tasks.
source: For example, neural activity in prefrontal and parietal cortex encodes stimuli during the delay period of working memory tasks, suggesting these areas contribute to maintaining the memory (Arnsten, 2011; Baeg et al., 2003; Erlich et al., 2015; Funahashi et al., 1989; Fuster and Alexander, 1971; Guo et al., 2014; Hanks et al., 2015; Harvey et al., 2012; Horst and Laubach, 2012; Jung et al., 1998; Kojima and Goldman-Rakic, 1982; Lak et al., 2014; Powell and Redish, 2014; Romo et al., 1999; Schoenbaum and Eichenbaum, 1995; Shadlen and Newsome, 2001; Spellman et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2013b; Yoon et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to prior literature.

claim: Prefrontal and parietal cortex contribute to maintaining working memory.
source: For example, neural activity in prefrontal and parietal cortex encodes stimuli during the delay period of working memory tasks, suggesting these areas contribute to maintaining the memory (Arnsten, 2011; Baeg et al., 2003; Erlich et al., 2015; Funahashi et al., 1989; Fuster and Alexander, 1971; Guo et al., 2014; Hanks et al., 2015; Harvey et al., 2012; Horst and Laubach, 2012; Jung et al., 1998; Kojima and Goldman-Rakic, 1982; Lak et al., 2014; Powell and Redish, 2014; Romo et al., 1999; Schoenbaum and Eichenbaum, 1995; Shadlen and Newsome, 2001; Spellman et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2013b; Yoon et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference from the cited literature about delay period encoding.

claim: Working memory emerges from the interaction between cortical and subcortical areas.
source: However, working memory is not implemented merely in cortex, but instead emerges from the interaction between cortical and subcortical areas (Floresco et al., 1997; Kopec et al., 2015; Parnaudeau et al., 2013), with the striatum as a key subcortical region.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The striatum is a key subcortical region for working memory.
source: However, working memory is not implemented merely in cortex, but instead emerges from the interaction between cortical and subcortical areas (Floresco et al., 1997; Kopec et al., 2015; Parnaudeau et al., 2013), with the striatum as a key subcortical region.
evidence: This is supported by citations and is a premise of the study.

claim: Human imaging studies have noted increased activation of the striatum during working memory tasks.
source: For example, human imaging studies have noted increased activation of the striatum during working memory tasks (Chang et al., 2007; Lewis et al., 2004; Olesen et al., 2004; Postle and D'Esposito, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to human imaging studies.

claim: In the primate caudate, metabolic activity and single cell recordings point to elevated activity during spatial working memory.
source: In addition, in the primate caudate, metabolic activity and single cell recordings point to elevated activity during spatial working memory (i.e. tasks that involve a memory for location) (Kermadi and Joseph, 1995; Levy et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to primate studies.

claim: Electric stimulation or lesions of the primate caudate leads to disruptions of spatial working memory.
source: Finally, electric stimulation or lesions of the primate caudate, as well as pharmacological silencing of the analogous region in rats, the dorsomedial striatum (DMS), leads to disruptions of spatial working memory (Balleine and O'Doherty, 2010; Cohen, 1972; Mordvinov, 1981; Rosvold and Delgado, 1956; Spencer et al., 2012; Stamm, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to lesion and stimulation studies.

claim: Pharmacological silencing of the dorsomedial striatum in rats leads to disruptions of spatial working memory.
source: Finally, electric stimulation or lesions of the primate caudate, as well as pharmacological silencing of the analogous region in rats, the dorsomedial striatum (DMS), leads to disruptions of spatial working memory (Balleine and O'Doherty, 2010; Cohen, 1972; Mordvinov, 1981; Rosvold and Delgado, 1956; Spencer et al., 2012; Stamm, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior rat studies.

claim: The dorsomedial striatum is the rat analog of the primate caudate.
source: Finally, electric stimulation or lesions of the primate caudate, as well as pharmacological silencing of the analogous region in rats, the dorsomedial striatum (DMS), leads to disruptions of spatial working memory (Balleine and O'Doherty, 2010; Cohen, 1972; Mordvinov, 1981; Rosvold and Delgado, 1956; Spencer et al., 2012; Stamm, 1969).
evidence: This is implied by the phrase 'the analogous region in rats, the dorsomedial striatum (DMS)' and is based on established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: Memory-encoding sequences have been observed in cortical and hippocampal areas in working memory tasks.
source: This is a reasonable hypothesis, given that (1) memory-encoding sequences have been observed in cortical and hippocampal areas in working memory tasks (Fujisawa et al., 2008; Harvey et al., 2012; Horst and Laubach, 2012; MacDonald et al., 2013; Pastalkova et al., 2008), and (2) the striatum is known to exhibit sequential activity in tasks that do not directly involve working memory (Lustig et al., 2005; Matell and Meck, 2000, 2004; Mello et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The striatum exhibits sequential activity in tasks that do not directly involve working memory.
source: This is a reasonable hypothesis, given that (1) memory-encoding sequences have been observed in cortical and hippocampal areas in working memory tasks (Fujisawa et al., 2008; Harvey et al., 2012; Horst and Laubach, 2012; MacDonald et al., 2013; Pastalkova et al., 2008), and (2) the striatum is known to exhibit sequential activity in tasks that do not directly involve working memory (Lustig et al., 2005; Matell and Meck, 2000, 2004; Mello et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Rats were trained on an operant delayed non-match to position (DNMP) task.
source: Rats were trained on an operant delayed non-match to position (DNMP) task (Figure 1A,B) (Dunnett et al., 1988).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods, illustrated in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The DNMP task involved delay periods of 1 s, 5 s, or 10 s, determined randomly.
source: The end of the delay period was signaled by the illumination of the nose port on the back wall of the chamber (delay period duration of 1 s, 5 s, or 10 s, determined randomly).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Rats spent the majority of their time at the nose port during the delay period.
source: During the delay period, the nose port remained inactive (i.e. the light in the nose port remained off and nose-poking has no effect), and the rats spent the majority of their time at the nose port (Figure 1B, bottom-center panel; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), waiting for the variable length delay period to terminate.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Rats' accuracy in the DNMP task declined with the length of the delay period.
source: Of note, the rats' accuracy in this task declined with the length of the delay period (p<10–4 repeated measures ANOVA, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The delay-dependence of accuracy provides validation that the short-term memory component of the task played a role in the rats' performance.
source: This delay-dependence provides validation that the short-term memory component of the task played a role in the rats' performance, as expected in a working memory task.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral data showing delay-dependent accuracy decline.

claim: Omission rates were low regardless of the length of the delay period (<10%).
source: In addition, omission rates and response latencies during the task revealed that the rats were highly engaged during the course of each trial. Omission rates were low regardless of the length of the delay period (<10%, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Median response latencies were short for all subjects for all 3 types of response.
source: In addition, median response latencies were short for all subjects for all 3 types of response (Figure 1D; median sample press latency < 3.5 s, median nose-poke latency < 1 s, median choice press latency < 3.5 s).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Muscimol infusion in the DMS caused a significant decline in choice accuracy compared to saline infusion.
source: We found a significant decline in choice accuracy with the infusion of muscimol in comparison to the infusion of saline (Figure 2B–C: p<0.001 effect for infusion day, repeated measures ANOVA, n = 7).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Muscimol infusion had no significant effect on median response latencies for rats.
source: Importantly, muscimol infusion had no significant effect on median response latencies for rats, suggesting minimal motor impairment (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Muscimol infusion in the DMS suggests minimal motor impairment.
source: Importantly, muscimol infusion had no significant effect on median response latencies for rats, suggesting minimal motor impairment (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of effect on response latencies.

claim: Muscimol infusion had no significant effect on the number of trials performed, sample omission rates, trial abort rates, sample bias, and choice bias across the population.
source: We also examined the effects of muscimol on the number of trials performed, sample omission rates, trial abort rates, sample bias, and choice bias and found that none of these measures were significantly affected by DMS inactivation across the population (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Wilcoxon signed rank test, n = 7).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A subset of rats performed fewer trials when treated with muscimol.
source: However, a subset of rats did perform fewer trials when treated with muscimol, which is consistent with the DMS being implicated in motivation or response vigor (Wang et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is an observation from the data with a citation to support the interpretation.

claim: The DMS is implicated in motivation or response vigor.
source: However, a subset of rats did perform fewer trials when treated with muscimol, which is consistent with the DMS being implicated in motivation or response vigor (Wang et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: 105 neurons were isolated from the DMS of 9 rats.
source: Spiking activity for 105 neurons was isolated from the DMS of 9 rats (summary of electrode localizations in Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collection.

claim: Between 5 and 25 units were recorded in each subject.
source: Between 5 and 25 units were recorded in each subject (Figure 3B, inset).
evidence: This is shown in the inset of Figure 3B.

claim: The average firing rates of DMS units tended to be low (population mean < 6 Hz).
source: The average firing rates of these units tended to be low (population mean < 6 Hz) (Figure 3B), consistent with previous reports of medium spiny neurons in the dorsal striatum (Berke, 2008; Berke et al., 2004; Mallet et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and citations to prior literature.

claim: Low firing rates are consistent with previous reports of medium spiny neurons in the dorsal striatum.
source: The average firing rates of these units tended to be low (population mean < 6 Hz) (Figure 3B), consistent with previous reports of medium spiny neurons in the dorsal striatum (Berke, 2008; Berke et al., 2004; Mallet et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neurons displayed sequential peaks of activity that spanned the entirety of the 10 s long delay period.
source: Neurons displayed sequential peaks of activity that spanned the entirety of the 10 s long delay period (Figure 4B, left panel).
evidence: This is shown in the heat-map in Figure 4B, left panel.

claim: The firing rates for the shorter delay trials displayed similar sequential activity throughout the delay period.
source: The firing rates for the shorter delay trials displayed similar sequential activity throughout the delay period (Figure 4B, middle and right panel), when ordered based on the peak times for the 10 s delay-duration trials (p<10–7, Spearman correlation test between peak times of 5 s-delay trials and 10 s-delay trials).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and statistical analysis.

claim: Peak times of 5 s-delay trials and 10 s-delay trials are significantly correlated.
source: The firing rates for the shorter delay trials displayed similar sequential activity throughout the delay period (Figure 4B, middle and right panel), when ordered based on the peak times for the 10 s delay-duration trials (p<10–7, Spearman correlation test between peak times of 5 s-delay trials and 10 s-delay trials).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (Spearman correlation test, p<10–7).

claim: The distribution of peak firing rate times in the real data revealed a bias towards the onset of the delay period.
source: In comparison to the shifted data, the distribution of peak firing rate times in the real data revealed a bias towards the onset of the delay period (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: There were more peaks towards the beginning of the delay period relative to what would be expected by chance.
source: In other words, although the sequences spanned the delay period, there were more peaks towards the beginning of the delay period relative to what would be expected by chance (p<0.01, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<0.01).

claim: Sequential activations of DMS neurons are not a by-product of responses to movement or position.
source: We therefore conclude that sequential activations of DMS neurons are not a by-product of responses to movement or position.
evidence: This conclusion is based on analyses controlling for position (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-D) and GLM analyses.

claim: Time from delay onset significantly improves the GLM model in 80% of the neurons (84/105) compared to a model with only position/locomotor variables.
source: Time from delay onset significantly improves the model in 80% of the neurons (84/105) in comparison to a model with only the position/locomotor variables (p<10–4, likelihood ratio test comparing models with and without time from delay period as predictor).
evidence: This is supported by GLM analysis and likelihood ratio test.

claim: Time-dependent changes in firing rates during the delay period cannot be accounted for by position or other tested variables.
source: This demonstrates that the time-dependent changes in firing rates during the delay period cannot be accounted for by position or the other variables we tested.
evidence: This is an inference from the GLM analysis results.

claim: Sequences were not specific to the delay period.
source: Note that sequences were not specific to the delay period, as we observed similar sequential activation of neurons when time-locking to other task events (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 53 of the 105 neurons showed significant encoding of the sample stimulus at some point during the delay period.
source: By this criteria, 53 of the 105 neurons showed significant encoding of the sample stimulus at some point during the delay period (p<0.01) with peak information values ranging between 0.07 to 0.69 bits (average peak information was 0.34 bits).
evidence: This is based on mutual information analysis with statistical significance testing.

claim: Peak information values for sample encoding neurons ranged between 0.07 to 0.69 bits.
source: By this criteria, 53 of the 105 neurons showed significant encoding of the sample stimulus at some point during the delay period (p<0.01) with peak information values ranging between 0.07 to 0.69 bits (average peak information was 0.34 bits).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from mutual information analysis.

claim: Average peak information for sample encoding neurons was 0.34 bits.
source: By this criteria, 53 of the 105 neurons showed significant encoding of the sample stimulus at some point during the delay period (p<0.01) with peak information values ranging between 0.07 to 0.69 bits (average peak information was 0.34 bits).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from mutual information analysis.

claim: The time of the peak sample information did not correlate significantly with the peak firing rate time.
source: Surprisingly, the sample information peaks did not display a sequential organization to match the peak firing rate sequence. In fact, the time of the peak sample information did not correlate significantly with the peak firing rate time (Figure 5C, Pearson correlation test; r=0.06, p=0.69).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (Pearson correlation test, r=0.06, p=0.69) and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: More than 80% of the stimulus encoding neurons (45/53) displayed peak information within the first 2 s of the delay period.
source: In fact, sample information most often peaked towards the onset of the delay period, with more than 80% of the stimulus encoding neurons (45/53) displaying peak information within the first 2 s of the delay period.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the mutual information analysis.

claim: Peak sample information was significantly earlier than peak activity.
source: On average, peak sample information was significantly earlier than peak activity (p<0.001; Wilcoxon signed rank test. Only neurons with significant information peaks were considered for this analysis).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon signed rank test, p<0.001).

claim: Sample decoding was highest at the onset of the delay period and declined over the course of the delay period.
source: In agreement with our findings from Figure 5, sample decoding was highest at the onset of the delay period (at the time of sample lever press) and declined over the course of the delay period (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A using population decoding analysis.

claim: Neural activity around the time of the sample lever press encodes the sample lever identity, as opposed to the rat's future choice.
source: This means that neural activity around the time of the sample lever press encodes the sample lever identity, as opposed to the rat's future choice.
evidence: This is inferred from the decoder performance on error trials shown in Figure 6B.

claim: At the time of the choice lever press, neural activity encoded the identity of the choice lever, as opposed to the sample identity.
source: In contrast, at the time of the choice lever press, neural activity encoded the identity of the choice lever, as opposed to the sample identity.
evidence: This is inferred from the decoder performance on error trials shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Head position is very similar across left and right sample trials following nose port arrival.
source: We show that head position is very similar across left and right sample trials following nose port arrival (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), yet our population decoder was able to decode the sample stimulus with high accuracy, even during the first 1.5 s when the rat strictly maintains its head position in front of the nose port (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The population decoder was able to decode the sample stimulus with high accuracy even during the first 1.5 s when the rat strictly maintains its head position in front of the nose port.
source: We show that head position is very similar across left and right sample trials following nose port arrival (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), yet our population decoder was able to decode the sample stimulus with high accuracy, even during the first 1.5 s when the rat strictly maintains its head position in front of the nose port (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: For more than 90% of neurons (95/105), the GLM model significantly improved when including the sample memory related variables.
source: For more than 90% of neurons (95/105), the model significantly improved when including the sample memory related variables (p<0.0001; Pearson's chi-squared test).
evidence: This is supported by GLM analysis and statistical testing.

claim: Many neurons differentiate between sample and choice presses in their encoding of lever identity.
source: We found that many neurons differentiate between sample and choice presses in their encoding of lever identity.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Some neurons preferentially encoded lever identity during the sample press while others encoded the lever identity during the choice press.
source: Much like the example neuron in Figure 7B, across the population of recorded neurons, some neurons preferentially encoded lever identity during the sample press while others encoded the lever identity during the choice press (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C.

claim: There was significantly more dispersion in the difference between sample and choice information than expected by chance.
source: There was significantly more dispersion in the difference between sample and choice information than expected by chance (inset in Figure 7C, p<10–5; two sample F-test for equality of variance for (sample information – choice information) in shuffled versus non-shuffled data).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (two sample F-test, p<10–5) shown in Figure 7C inset.

claim: DMS firing patterns are not merely reflecting position or motor actions.
source: This analysis supports the conclusion that DMS firing patterns are not merely reflecting position or motor actions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Stronger stimulus encoding toward the onset of the delay period has been reported in studies of primate cortical regions.
source: Stronger stimulus encoding toward the onset of the delay period has been reported in studies of primate cortical regions, although those studies did not compare sample stimulus encoding to sequential firing activity (Brody et al., 2003; Bruce et al., 1985; Clark et al., 2012; Colby et al., 1996; Gregoriou et al., 2012; Romo et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Previous recordings in primates have reported sustained delay period activity that encodes short-term memory in a subset of caudate neurons with delay periods of 2–4 s.
source: Indeed, previous recordings in primates have reported sustained delay period activity that encodes short-term memory in a subset of caudate neurons with delay periods of 2–4 s (Hikosaka et al., 1989; Kawagoe et al., 1998; Schultz and Romo, 1988; Schultz et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior primate studies.

claim: Some neurons showed stimulus encoding during the delay period that persisted for several seconds.
source: In our study, we observed some neurons with stimulus encoding during the delay period that persisted for several seconds, in agreement with prior work.
evidence: This is an observation from the data, consistent with prior literature.

claim: No single neuron was found to encode the sample stimulus for the entire duration of the delay period.
source: However, no single neuron was found to encode the sample stimulus for the entire duration of the delay period (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Striatal neurons differentially encode the sample press and the choice press.
source: This revealed that striatal neurons differentially encode the sample press and the choice press, and that encoding of the same action is dependent on the context of the action within the task.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Encoding of the same action is dependent on the context of the action within the task.
source: This revealed that striatal neurons differentially encode the sample press and the choice press, and that encoding of the same action is dependent on the context of the action within the task.
evidence: This is an inference from the differential encoding of sample vs. choice presses shown in Figure 7.

claim: The striatum is involved in encoding memories of task-related variables, and not merely encoding the rats' position or movement during the task.
source: This supports the idea that the striatum is involved in encoding memories of task-related variables, and not merely encoding the rats' position or movement during the task.
evidence: This is an inference from the context-dependent encoding shown in Figure 7.

claim: The striatum may be involved in initiating the storage of new memories in cortical networks, an idea often referred to as 'gating'.
source: For example, it has been suggested that the striatum may be involved in initiating the storage of new memories in cortical networks, an idea often referred to as 'gating' (Baier et al., 2010; Frank et al., 2001; Gruber et al., 2006; O'Reilly and Frank, 2006; Braver and Cohen 2000).
evidence: This is a theoretical model from prior literature as indicated by citations.

claim: According to the gating model, the striatum plays a role in selecting cortical memory buffers that are to be updated and determines the time memory updating occurs.
source: According to this idea, the striatum plays a role in selecting cortical memory buffers that are to be updated and determines the time memory updating occurs, similar to the role the striatum is thought to play in initiating and selecting motor actions (Bailey and Mair, 2006; Bhutani et al., 2013; Grillner et al., 2005; Kropotov and Etlinger, 1999; Mink, 1996).
evidence: This is a theoretical model from prior literature as indicated by citations.

claim: The gating model ascribes a crucial role to the striatum at the onset of the delay period, when new information must be stored in short-term memory buffers.
source: The gating model ascribes a crucial role to the striatum at the onset of the delay period, when new information must be stored in short-term memory buffers (Baier et al., 2010; Frank et al., 2001; Gruber et al., 2006; O'Reilly and Frank, 2006; Braver and Cohen 2000).
evidence: This is a theoretical model from prior literature as indicated by citations.

claim: The data emphasizes the importance of the striatum at the beginning of the delay period, as the stimulus is most strongly encoded during that period.
source: Interestingly, our data emphasizes the importance of the striatum at the beginning of the delay period, as the stimulus is most strongly encoded during that period.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings in relation to the gating model.

claim: Activity in the DMS might be sufficient to support the animal's behavior.
source: Although the accuracy of our population decoder decreases substantially during the course of the delay period, the decoding accuracy near the end of the delay period is roughly comparable to behavioral performance even at the 10 s delays (Figure 1C and Figure 6A), indicating that activity in the DMS might be sufficient to support the animal's behavior.
evidence: This is speculation based on comparing decoder accuracy to behavioral performance.

claim: The DMS could assist cortical areas in maintaining the memory throughout the delay period, irrespective of holding the content of the memory.
source: As another possibility, the DMS could assist cortical areas in maintaining the memory throughout the delay period, irrespective of holding the content of the memory.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: Memory encoding activity in cortex often appears as persistent elevated activity or sequential activations of neurons.
source: Memory encoding activity in cortex often appears as persistent elevated activity or sequential activations of neurons (Baeg et al., 2003; Cromer et al., 2011; Fujisawa et al., 2008; Fuster and Alexander, 1971; Hanks et al., 2015; Harvey et al., 2012; Horst and Laubach, 2012; Kojima and Goldman-Rakic, 1982; MacDonald et al., 2013; Pastalkova et al., 2008; Powell and Redish, 2014; Schoenbaum and Eichenbaum, 1995), which may be implemented using positive feedback through distributed cortico-striato-thalamic loops (Alexander et al., 1986; Houk and Wise, 1995; Middleton and Strick, 2000, 2002; Wang, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Memory encoding in cortex may be implemented using positive feedback through distributed cortico-striato-thalamic loops.
source: Memory encoding activity in cortex often appears as persistent elevated activity or sequential activations of neurons (Baeg et al., 2003; Cromer et al., 2011; Fujisawa et al., 2008; Fuster and Alexander, 1971; Hanks et al., 2015; Harvey et al., 2012; Horst and Laubach, 2012; Kojima and Goldman-Rakic, 1982; MacDonald et al., 2013; Pastalkova et al., 2008; Powell and Redish, 2014; Schoenbaum and Eichenbaum, 1995), which may be implemented using positive feedback through distributed cortico-striato-thalamic loops (Alexander et al., 1986; Houk and Wise, 1995; Middleton and Strick, 2000, 2002; Wang, 2001).
evidence: This is a theoretical model from prior literature as indicated by citations.

claim: The sequential activity that spans the delay period in DMS could play a role in exciting cortical memory buffers and enabling memory encoding activity there.
source: In this view, the sequential activity that spans the delay period in DMS could play a role in exciting cortical memory buffers and enabling memory encoding activity there.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of the observed sequences.

claim: The stimulus memory may be stored in the striatum in a form that would not be fully detectable in the spiking activity, perhaps in short-term synaptic plasticity.
source: As yet another possibility, the stimulus memory may be stored in the striatum in a form that would not be fully detectable in the spiking activity, perhaps in short-term synaptic plasticity, as suggested by recent theoretical models (Lundqvist et al., 2010; Mongillo et al., 2008; Stokes, 2015).
evidence: This is speculation based on theoretical models from prior literature.

claim: Sequential neural activity dynamics have been reported in the striatum in tasks that do not involve spatial working memory.
source: Sequential neural activity dynamics have been reported in the striatum in tasks that do not involve spatial working memory (Lustig et al., 2005; Matell and Meck, 2000, 2004; Mello et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The delay-period spanning sequences in DMS support a general role for the striatum in time keeping, rather than a specific role in working memory.
source: These studies, taken together with our finding that firing rate sequences we observed here were dissociated from stimulus encoding activity (Figure 5B,C), suggests that the delay-period spanning sequences in DMS support a general role for the striatum in time keeping, rather than a specific role in working memory.
evidence: This is an inference from the current findings combined with prior literature.

claim: Cortical and hippocampal areas display stimulus encoding sequences that span the delay period.
source: In particular, cortical (Astrand et al., 2015; Cromer et al., 2011; Crowe et al., 2010; Fujisawa et al., 2008; Harvey et al., 2012; Horst and Laubach, 2012) and hippocampal (MacDonald et al., 2013; Pastalkova et al., 2008) areas display stimulus encoding sequences that span the delay period.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The neural dynamics in the DMS suggest a different role for the striatum in working memory relative to cortex and hippocampus.
source: This suggests a different role for the striatum in working memory relative to these other regions.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the current findings to prior literature on cortex and hippocampus.

claim: Cortex and hippocampus may be involved in maintaining the memory throughout the delay period, whereas the striatum may be involved in initiating memory storage.
source: Specifically, cortex and hippocampus may be involved in maintaining the memory throughout the delay period, whereas the striatum may be involved in initiating memory storage.
evidence: This is speculation based on comparing the current findings to prior literature.

claim: Ridge-to-background ratios were significantly greater than chance level for all delay period lengths.
source: Ridge to-background ratios were significantly greater than chance level for all delay period lengths (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, p<0.001; one tailed test using the ratios from the randomly shifted data as the null distribution).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Even when controlling for the rats' position by excluding times that they were not at the nose port, sequences were evident that closely matched the sequences based on the full dataset.
source: We found that even when controlling for the rats' position by excluding times that they were not at the nose port, sequences were evident that closely matched the sequences based on the full dataset (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The presence of firing rate sequences was statistically significant, even when using only data from times when the rat was at the nose port.
source: Ridge-to-background analysis confirmed that the presence of firing rate sequences was statistically significant, even when using only data from times when the rat was at the nose port (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ridge-to-background analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Muscimol infusion was significantly impaired for the 5 s and 10 s delay trials but not for 1 s delay trials.
source: Accuracy was significantly impaired for the 5 s and 10 s delay trials (*p<0.05; Wilcoxon signed rank test) but not for 1 s delay trials (p=0.38; Wilcoxon signed rank test, n=7 rats).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C with statistical analysis.

claim: Peak activity time when rat was in the nose port was significantly correlated with peak activity time calculated using all data when aligned to first nose port arrival.
source: Peak activity time when rat was in the nose port (left plot of panel A) was significantly correlated with peak activity time calculated using all data (middle plot of panel A) (r = 0.87, p<10–6 Pearson correlation test).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B with statistical analysis.

claim: Peak activity time when rat was in the nose port was significantly correlated with peak activity time calculated using all data when aligned to delay period onset.
source: Peak activity time when rat was in the nose port (left plot of panel B) was significantly correlated with peak activity time calculated using all data (middle plot of panel B) (r = 0.74, p<10–6 Pearson correlation test).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D with statistical analysis.
